title: Keep Me as the Apple of Your Eye
summary: David, surrounded by enemies who hunt him like lions, asks God to hear a case he believes is just. He protests that his heart has been tested and found faithful, begs God to hide him in the shadow of his wings, and calls on the LORD to rise and confront the wicked. The psalm ends with a contrast: his enemies have their portion in this life, but he will be satisfied with the sight of God's face.
story: Psalm 17 sits in Book I of the Psalter (Psalms 1 to 41), a collection made up almost entirely of psalms headed with David's name. It follows Psalm 16, a quiet song of trust that ends in the joy of God's presence, and it takes up the same longing in a far more dangerous situation. The prayer's heading calls it a prayer (tefillah), one of only a handful of psalms given that label, and the whole psalm is exactly that: an appeal lodged with the judge of the world by someone who has nowhere else to go. It prepares the reader for Psalm 18, where David looks back on deliverance from the same kind of enemies and sings about how God answered.
historical:
The superscription reads simply A prayer of David. The Hebrew phrase translated of David can mean written by David, belonging to a Davidic collection, dedicated to David, or written about or in the manner of David, and scholars differ on how much weight to give the headings. Jewish and Christian tradition has generally read them as statements of authorship. Many modern scholars regard them as ancient notes added when the psalms were collected, valuable as early interpretation but not necessarily original to the poems. The psalm itself names no event. Its picture of a man tracked down and surrounded fits the years when Saul pursued David through the wilderness of Judah (1 Samuel 23 to 26), and many readers have heard it against that background, though the text doesn't require it.

Some scholars have suggested that psalms like this one were prayed at the sanctuary by a person falsely accused, who came before God for a verdict when human courts could not settle the case. Solomon's temple prayer provides for exactly that situation, when a man swears an oath before the altar and asks God to judge between him and his accuser (1 Kings 8:31-32). The language of vindication, testing by night, and a morning answer in verse 15 would fit such a setting well.
cultural:
Two images in verse 8 come from Israel's older songs. The phrase “the apple of Your eye” renders a Hebrew idiom for the pupil, literally the little man of the eye, the small reflected figure you see when you look into someone's eye. The pupil is the part of the body a person guards most instinctively, and Moses' song uses the same idiom for God's care of Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:10). The shadow of God's wings echoes the next verse of that song, where God is like an eagle over its young, and it may also recall the winged cherubim over the ark in the Most Holy Place, the innermost room of the sanctuary. Either way, the image is shelter by nearness.

The courtroom was a familiar part of ancient life, conducted at the town gate before elders. A righteous plea in verse 1 is a legal term for a just case. David is not claiming sinless perfection. He is claiming that in this dispute he is in the right, and he asks the highest judge to examine the evidence. Lions, which then still lived in the thickets of the Jordan valley and the hill country, were the natural picture of a predator who waits in ambush.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament, the most common type of psalm in the Psalter: a cry to God in trouble, usually moving through complaint, petition, and a statement of trust. Here the structure falls into three movements, each opening with an appeal to God: hear my plea (verses 1 to 5), show your loving devotion and keep me (verses 6 to 12), and arise and confront them (verses 13 to 15). Hebrew poetry works mainly by parallelism, in which the second line of a pair repeats, sharpens, or extends the first, and the psalm is full of it: “Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings”. The words for eyes, lips, mouth, and face recur throughout, so that the psalm becomes a contest of looking. God's eyes see what is right (verse 2), the enemies' eyes are set to cast him down (verse 11), and the psalmist ends by beholding God's face (verse 15).

outline.t: A just case laid before God, who has tested the heart
A plea for protection from enemies who hunt like lions
Arise, O LORD: the men whose portion is in this life

doctrines.note: The psalm models prayer as bringing a real case to God, with argument and evidence, rather than vague piety. It assumes God listens, weighs, and acts, and that it is right to ask him to.
God is pictured as the judge who tests hearts by night and whose verdict comes from his presence. The psalmist entrusts vengeance to God rather than taking it himself.

Verse 15 sets the greatest good not in wealth or children but in beholding God's face. Whether it speaks of a morning after a night of prayer or of waking beyond death, it points the reader past the goods of this life.

words.note: Tsedeq, righteousness or rightness. In a legal setting it means a just cause, being in the right. It frames the psalm from the first line (“my righteous plea”) to the last (“I will behold Your face in righteousness”). The psalmist is not boasting of moral perfection but asking God to recognize that his cause is just.

Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love, covenant loyalty. It is the love that keeps faith with a relationship over time, especially when the other party has no claim to force it. In verse 7 the psalmist appeals not only to his own innocence but to this settled loyalty of God, the ground beneath all his other arguments.

Ishon, the pupil of the eye, literally a little man, from the tiny image of a person reflected in someone's eye. The same idiom appears in Deuteronomy 32:10 and Proverbs 7:2. The picture is of something guarded by reflex, protected before a person even thinks about it.

Quts, to awake. When I awake in verse 15 may mean waking in the morning after a night vigil at the sanctuary, when the verdict or the sense of God's presence came. Many Christian and some Jewish interpreters have also heard in it the hope of waking from the sleep of death, as in Daniel 12:2, where the same verb is used.

christ: The psalm's claim of a righteous plea from lips free of deceit fits no ordinary petitioner perfectly, and Christians have long heard in it the voice of the one who truly could say it. Peter describes Jesus as one who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, and who, when insulted, entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:22-23). That is the posture of this psalm: surrounded, falsely accused, handing the case to God. Jesus also used the image of verse 8 about himself, longing to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37). This is a thematic link rather than a prediction, but it is a real one. The psalm's final hope, to behold God's face and be satisfied, is what the New Testament promises to those who belong to Christ, who will see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

hard.q: Isn't it self-righteous to tell God that he has tested you and found no evil?
hard.a: It can sound that way to readers who know Psalm 51 or Romans 3. But the psalmist is speaking in a courtroom, about a specific accusation, not offering a verdict on his whole life. In Israel's law a person could be innocent of a charge while still needing forgiveness for many other things, and the Psalter holds both prayers side by side. Some interpreters add that such protests of innocence express covenant loyalty: the psalmist has kept to God's paths rather than joining the violent, and he asks God to act on the covenant. Christians have also read these protests as finally true only of Christ, and as prayed by his people in union with him. Either way, the psalm does not ask God to reward merit. It asks him to see clearly and to judge justly, and it ends by wanting God himself more than vindication.

questions: Have you ever been accused of something you didn't do? What would it look like to bring that case to God rather than only to other people?
The enemies in verse 14 have their portion in this life. What would it look like for your satisfaction to rest in God's presence rather than in what you can store up?
The psalmist asks to be kept like the apple of God's eye. How does it change prayer to believe you are guarded that closely?
